segments.text: Abnormal psychology studies patterns of thought, emotion and behaviour associated with significant distress, dysfunction or other clinically relevant problems. Clinical psychology applies assessment and psychological intervention to these problems.
This area requires careful language. Disorders are not moral weaknesses, and diagnosis cannot be made from one symptom or casual observation.

items.text: Concept of abnormality
: Judgments about abnormality may consider distress, dysfunction, danger, deviance from norms and context. No single criterion is sufficient in every case.
Causes
: Modern explanations commonly use a biopsychosocial approach: biological vulnerability, psychological processes and social/environmental conditions may interact.
Clinical assessment
: Assessment may combine interview, behavioural observation, psychological tests and relevant history. The aim is to understand the person and guide decisions, not merely attach a label.
Schizophrenia spectrum
: Schizophrenia involves disturbances that can affect perception, thinking, motivation and functioning. Do not equate schizophrenia with “split personality.”
Mood disorders
: Mood disorders involve significant disturbances in mood, such as depressive or bipolar patterns. Precise diagnosis requires criteria, duration and functional context.
Anxiety disorders
: Anxiety disorders involve excessive fear/anxiety and related behaviours that differ in their triggers and patterns. Normal anxiety should not automatically be pathologized.
Personality disorders
: Personality disorders involve enduring patterns that are inflexible, pervasive and associated with impairment or distress. They should not be used as casual labels.
Psychological treatment

: Psychological therapies include approaches such as cognitive-behavioural, behavioural, psychodynamic, humanistic and family/group methods. Treatment choice depends on the problem, evidence, person and context.

segments.text: The following sections develop the compressed source notes into the academic depth needed for first-time understanding and analytical answer writing.

Psychological disorders are patterns of cognition, emotion or behaviour associated with significant distress, impairment or clinically relevant risk within a cultural and developmental context. No single criterion such as rarity or social deviance is sufficient. A behaviour can be unusual without being disordered, and distress can be understandable without meeting diagnostic criteria.

items.text: Dimensional thinking

: Many symptoms vary by degree rather than appearing as completely separate categories. Diagnostic categories remain useful for communication and service organization, but dimensional severity and functioning are also important.
Culture and context

: The meaning of symptoms can vary across cultures, and clinicians must distinguish culturally expected beliefs or practices from psychopathology. Diagnostic systems such as DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 include cultural and contextual guidance.
Biological contributors
: Genetic vulnerability, neurodevelopment, illness, sleep, substances and physiological systems can contribute to risk. Biological influence does not mean a disorder is fully determined by biology.
Psychological contributors
: Learning histories, coping style, attention, interpretation, emotion regulation and beliefs can affect onset or maintenance.
Social contributors

: Trauma, poverty, isolation, discrimination, relationship conflict and chronic stress can alter risk and recovery. Social factors should be treated as part of the explanation rather than background decoration.
Diathesis-stress
: A vulnerability may remain unexpressed until combined with sufficient stress, while protective factors may reduce risk. This model explains why similar stressors do not affect everyone identically.
Clinical interview

: A structured or semi-structured interview gathers symptoms, onset, duration, functioning, risk, history and context. Good assessment asks what a symptom means in the person's life rather than simply checking boxes.
Behavioural and psychological measures
: Standardized scales, cognitive testing and behavioural observations can supplement interviews. Results must be interpreted within their validated purpose and population.
Differential diagnosis
: Similar symptoms can arise from different disorders, medical conditions, substances or normal responses. Diagnosis therefore requires pattern, duration, exclusion criteria and functional context.
Risk assessment
: Assessment of self-harm, violence or vulnerability requires specific evidence and professional judgment. It produces risk estimates and management plans, not certainty about future behaviour.

blocks.text: Major disorder groups in the syllabus

items.text: Schizophrenia spectrum

: Schizophrenia can involve delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thought or behaviour, negative symptoms and cognitive difficulties. It is not 'split personality'. Causes are multifactorial, and treatment often combines medication, psychosocial support and rehabilitation.
Depressive disorders

: Depression involves sustained patterns of low mood or loss of interest together with cognitive, physical and functional symptoms. Ordinary sadness is not automatically a disorder; duration, severity and impairment matter.
Bipolar disorders
: Bipolar conditions involve episodes of abnormally elevated or irritable mood and increased activation, with depressive episodes in many cases. Mania is not simply feeling energetic or happy.
Anxiety-related disorders

: Anxiety disorders differ in the object and pattern of fear, avoidance and physiological arousal. Examples include generalized anxiety, panic disorder, phobic disorders and social anxiety. Exposure-based and cognitive-behavioural interventions have strong evidence for several anxiety conditions.
Personality disorders

: These involve enduring, inflexible patterns across cognition, affect, relationships and impulse control that cause impairment or distress. They require careful longitudinal assessment and must not be used as casual insults.
Cognitive-behavioural therapies

: CBT approaches identify links among thoughts, emotions and behaviour and use structured methods such as behavioural activation, exposure, skills practice and cognitive reappraisal. Specific techniques are matched to the problem rather than applied identically to everyone.
Behavioural therapies
: Behavioural approaches use learning principles to change avoidance, habits and environmental contingencies. Exposure is a central evidence-based method for several fear-related problems.
Psychodynamic therapies
: Modern psychodynamic therapies focus on recurring relationship patterns, affect and less conscious processes. Evidence varies by condition and treatment form.
Humanistic/person-centred approaches
: These emphasize empathy, therapeutic relationship, authenticity and the client's subjective experience. Relationship quality is important across many therapies, even when techniques differ.
Integrated care

: Psychological, medical and social interventions can be combined when indicated. Evidence-based practice integrates research evidence, clinical expertise and the person's characteristics, culture, values and preferences.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Define abnormal and clinical psychology, discuss criteria and causes, explain assessment, cover the major disorder groups in the syllabus, and finish with psychological interventions and ethical care.
• American Psychiatric Association, DSM-5-TR (2022); World Health Organization, ICD-11.
• Abnormality must be understood in context.
• Assessment should combine information rather than rely on one sign.
• Mental disorders have multiple possible contributing factors.
• Evidence-based psychological treatment can reduce distress and improve functioning.
• Connect definitions with mechanisms, examples and limitations; do not present the topic as a list of isolated terms.
